paper_title: The Optimizer Is the Agent: Reasoning-Driven Search across Prompts, Programs, and ML Workflows

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent systems for optimizing prompts, programs, and ML workflows typically rely on explicit outer-loop controllers such as evolutionary search, bandits, or textual-gradient methods. We ask a fundamentally different question: how much of this search policy can be internalized by a single tool-using agent? We present ReASearch, a unified framework for reasoning-driven optimization in which the agent autonomously decides what to evaluate, how to diagnose failures, which edits to make, and when to verify or restart. Rather than serving only as a proposal generator guided by hand-designed heuristics, the agent actively analyzes outcomes, allocates budget, and refines its strategy over long horizons through persistent memory. With a shared agent loop and domain-specific tools, ReASearch instantiates the exact same scaffold to optimize prompts, programs, and ML workflows. Across 14 diverse tasks, it is competitive with and mostly better than specialized optimization systems, achieving gains of 2% to 40% over strong domain-specific baselines, and in some cases discovering solutions that improve on prior human best-known results. Crucially, we observe that complex search behaviors, which are typically implemented by explicit controllers, emerge naturally from the agent's reasoning process.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Optimizing text-based artifacts, such as system prompts, programs, and training configurations, is central challenge in modern AI. Traditional optimization methods often struggle in these settings because they operate over large, discrete spaces while lacking access to the rich semantic structure of natural language and code. This limitation has motivated growing body of work that uses large language models as semantic optimizers: LLMs propose structured edits based on execution feedback, while external search mechanisms such as Bayesian optimization (Kang & Yoganarasimhan, 2025; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024; Schneider et al., 2024; Bergstra et al., 2011), bandits (Cemri et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Pryzant et al., 2023), and evolutionary search (Secheresse et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2023; Fernando et al., 2023) guide exploration and selection. This line of research has advanced rapidly, encompassing controllers that range from prompting-based methods that optimize against score histories (Yang et al., 2023), to textualgradient frameworks (Khattab et al., 2023; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024; Yin & Wang, 2025), to planningand evolution-based systems that maintain candidate sets and search over revisions (Wang et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2025; Novikov et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2026), as well as LLM-generated adaptive controllers for meta-heuristics Zelikman et al. (2023); Van Stein & Back (2024); Shi et al. (2026). Yet across this diversity, central design choice remains largely unchallenged: most strategic search decisions still live outside the model. Work done during internship at Snowflake. These authors contributed equally and share last authorship. 1 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 Figure 1: Positioning ReASearch relative to existing methods. The external algorithmic controller decides which candidate to branch from, which evaluations to run, how to allocate budget, and how to recover from stagnation; the LLM merely contributes semantic edits within that hard-coded loop. This leaves open more fundamental question than whether LLMs can optimize at all: how much of the search policy can be internalized by single reasoning agent? We study this question through Reasoning-driven Agentic Search (ReASearch), controllerlight framework that places tool-using LLM agent fully in charge of the optimization loop. While recent proof-of-concept projects have demonstrated agents automating specific ML pipelines, ReASearch provides systematic evaluation of internalized search across diverse modalities. The agent is equipped with domain-specific tools for evaluation, analysis, editing, and memory across three distinct settings: prompt optimization, program evolution, and ML workflow optimization. There is no fixed outer-loop search procedure: core optimization operations are all packaged as tools. The agent decides what to test next, when to verify, when to revert, and when to stop exploring to exploit stronger candidate. We provide concise comparison of ReASearch with existing methods in Figure 1. Across benchmark suite spanning 14 tasks, the same agent scaffold is highly competitive with specialized systems built around explicit search procedures. Furthermore, its trajectories exhibit recurring optimizer-like behaviors that are not hard-coded in the controller: double-verification of promising gains, reuse of similar past failures, deliberate reverting after unproductive branches, and adaptive exploration. These results suggest that, given rich-feedback environments, frontier tool-using agents can internalize substantial fraction of the search logic previously delegated to external mathematical meta-heuristics. Contributions. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We cast text-based optimization as sequential reasoning problem and present ReASearch, unified, controller-light agent framework for optimizing prompts, programs, and ML workflows using single shared agent design. Across three distinct domains and 14 diverse tasks, ReASearch consistently matches or outperforms strong, domain-specific baselines (by 2% to 40%) within the same budgets, and in some cases discovers solutions surpassing prior human best-known results. We conduct systematic analysis of agent trajectories and identify recurring reasoning patterns that emerge during search, including candidate verification, hypothesis-driven revision, reuse of prior lessons, revert-based recovery, and adaptive exploration under budget constraints. These behaviors arise without any additional heuristic control. 2 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 Figure 2: Prior methods use LLMs primarily as mutators, with candidate selection and optimization goals determined by external heuristic algorithms. In contrast, ReASearch exposes the entire optimization process through tools, giving the agent full control over the search procedure and enabling it to solve wide range of tasks.

sections.title: 1.1 Related Work
sections.content: ReASearch relates to LLM-based text optimization, autonomous ML agents, and code agents; across these, the recurring pattern is an external controller that owns the search policy while the LLM contributes only local edits. We defer detailed discussion to Appendix A.

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: We formulate the objective (2.1), present the general agent architecture (2.2), and describe domain-specific tool designs for 3 task categories (2.3) with details in Appendix G.

sections.title: 2.1 Problem formulation
sections.content: Let denote the space of textual artifacts, such as prompts, programs, and training configurations. Given task instance and an artifact Z, the system generates an output P( x, z) with reward r(x, Y). Our objective is to find arg max zZ (cid:104) xD YP(x,z)[r(x, Y)] (cid:105) . (1) This formulation is general and naturally simplifies to task-free optimization as special case. In scenarios where the objective is independent of specific input instances x, such as in algorithmic discovery or geometric optimization tasks, the outer expectation over vanishes. Consequently, the goal reduces to maximizing the expected reward of the artifact itself. The key challenge is how to search Z. Prior work typically uses external meta-heuristics, such as evolutionary algorithms, bandits, or textual gradient methods. We ask whether an LLM agent with appropriate tools can instead perform this search through reasoning alone.

sections.title: 2.2 General agent architecture
sections.content: We implement simple code agent with basic file I/O, Python/Bash execution, and lightweight memory module. At each turn, the agent receives system prompt encoding domain guidance and the current optimization state, along with its interaction history, and reasons about which tool to invoke next. The core loop itself is task-agnostic: all task-specific information is provided through two interfaces only, the tool set AT and the task-specific system prompt. As result, the same agent can optimize prompts, programs, and training scripts by changing only the available tools and the prompt. Among all these tools, python exec is the most important: it transforms the agent from pure text reasoner into computational reasoner that can write analysis scripts, compute statistics over evaluation 3 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 Figure 3: We visualize an example agent trajectory for prompt optimization, highlighting automatic verification and final prompt selection. None of this process is hardcoded; it emerges from the guiding instruction, with agents freely deciding each next step. logs, and programmatically identify failure patterns. Figure 2 visualizes our framework and compares it with prior methods. Context management and memory To support long-horizon optimization, we equip the agent with both context compression and persistent memory. When token usage exceeds threshold, or when the agent chooses to prune its context, it invokes compaction tool to summarize the interaction history. The agent also maintains persistent lessons.md file and is periodically prompted to read from or update it. This file records the most important lessons from the run, including what worked, what failed, and what to try next, along with key empirical observations, such as which methods achieved which levels of performance under which conditions.

sections.title: 2.3.1 Prompt optimization.
sections.content: Tools The agent optimizes system prompt for student LLM on dataset with train, validation, and test splits. Unlike prior hard-coded pipelines that repeatedly sample random training minibatches, revise the prompt, and validate new proposals, we expose training and validation evaluation as tools that the agent can invoke adaptively based on its reasoning and remaining budget. First, get next minibatch samples the next minibatch of training examples, where is chosen by the agent according to its current budget. Second, call student model batch evaluates prompt candidate on specified batch of example indices, which may correspond either to newly sampled training examples or to previously identified difficult cases. The agent has access to the full evaluation trajectories on these training examples. Third, validate candidate evaluates prompt candidate on the validation set and returns only aggregate accuracy, without per-example trajectories, to reduce overfitting to validation feedback. In addition, the agent can call the generalpurpose python exec tool to inspect prior evaluation results, compute summary statistics, and perform more detailed diagnosis. Variance-robust effective verification The full autonomy is especially important because prompt evaluation is often high variance, making purely metric-based control brittle. Figure 3 illustrates representative agent trajectory for prompt optimization. With access to the tools, the agent naturally adapts its search strategy. For example, we observe the agent 4 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 Figure 4: Program evolution and ML workflow optimization exhibit similar patterns: the agent actively uses Python for reasoning and small-scale experiments before running expensive evaluations, while delegating targeted code edits to separate agent to keep the main agents context clean. rechecking promising prompt candidates on additional training samples before validation, analyzing whether gains reflect genuine capability improvements or superficial pattern matching, examining score trajectories across diverse examples to assess robustness, and deliberately probing edge cases corresponding to earlier failure modes. Behaviors that would previously require hand-designed algorithmic components instead emerge directly from reasoning over the evaluation history. Final prompt selection The final prompt is not determined solely by the candidate with the best validation metric, as is typical in prior work. Instead, after the optimization run, the final agent turn is instructed to select the final prompt, or synthesize new one, by reasoning over the full evaluation history and the lessons accumulated throughout the run. This is especially useful in data-scarce settings such as AIME and Terminal-Bench, where validation feedback can be highly variable. In such cases, we observe that the agents final choice can outperform the prompt with the highest validation score on the test set.

sections.title: 2.3.2 Program evolution.
sections.content: The agent optimizes program for single hard problem, such as challenging optimization task or pattern induction problem in ARC-AGI-2 (Chollet et al., 2025), where fundamentally different algorithmic strategies may all be plausible. This setting requires the agent to explore diverse approaches, reason about why one strategy outperforms another on particular problem structures, and accumulate insights across attempts. These requirements align naturally with the strengths of our framework. Tools As in prompt optimization, program evaluation is exposed as tool, evaluate, which the agent can invoke whenever it deems appropriate. At the start of the run, the agent reads the baseline program. Thereafter, whenever it decides to modify the program, it calls the edit code tool, which routes the requested changes to separate subagent that applies the edit while keeping the main agent context clean. We additionally use verification subagent that checks whether each edit is valid and respects task constraints. Higher-level analysis and diagnosis are deliberately kept inside the main agent: this preserves reasoning context across turns (which can be compacted into useful memory), avoids information loss between agents, and reduces coordination complexity. Figure 4 illustrates this pattern, which program evolution and ML workflow optimization share. Lesson accumulation and sub-program-based analysis Compared with prior evolutionary systems, our framework offers two main advantages. First, the cycle of repeated attempts and lesson accumulation enables the agent to improve continuously on difficult tasks. Rather than treating each mutation as an isolated step, the agent can form and re5 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 fine hypotheses over time by integrating evidence across many trials. Second, the agent can make extensive use of the general-purpose python exec tool to inspect intermediate behavior, analyze outputs, test subcomponents in isolation, and reason directly about the structure of the problem. This allows it to move beyond shallow mutation and perform deliberate diagnosis, verification, and refinement.

sections.title: 2.3.3 ML workflow optimization.
sections.content: This category covers machine learning training tasks in which improvement may come from many sources, including hyperparameter tuning, feature engineering, architectural changes, loss design, optimizer choice, and regularization. The agent reads the training code, runs limited-duration experiments via run experiment, observes the resulting metrics and training dynamics, and proposes targeted modifications to address the current bottlenecks. The overall tool design is similar to that in program evolution, but the instructions and execution pipeline are specialized for ML workflows. Rich but efficient and effective exploration Unlike prior black-box hyperparameter search, the agent operates directly on the training workflow itself. Because it can read and reason about the code, it can decide which part of the pipeline to modify, whether adjusting hyperparameters, changing the learning-rate schedule, adding regularization, revising the architecture, or switching optimizers. With python exec, it can further analyze training curves, diagnose instability or overfitting, estimate feasible model sizes under compute or memory constraints, and compare evidence across runs using its persistent lessons and experimental history.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate our agent framework on 14 diverse tasks across 3 categories. In each category, we compare our general-purpose framework against the state-of-the-art methods for that task category and demonstrate its advantages, while using comparable budget and requiring only minimal task-specific tuning beyond the domain-level system prompt template. For each setting, we conduct 3 independent runs and report the average. See the detailed task introduction, data split, and hyper-parameters of each setting in Appendix H. We first present tool-call overall frequency statistics for each category in Figure 5. The results highlight characteristic pattern of ReASearch: the agent spends most of its time on reasoning rather than execution, which is typically more expensive. In prompt and program optimization, more than 70% of tool calls are devoted to reasoning with Python. In ML workflow optimization, Python accounts for smaller fraction of calls, but as we show later through specific examples, it remains critical to the agents strongest results. Figure 5: Tool call frequency statistics for each category.

sections.title: 3.1 Prompt optimization
sections.content: Settings The agent optimizes system prompts for student LLMs across three domains: mathematical reasoning (AIME 2025, GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021)), multi-hop question answering (HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018)), and software engineering (Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026)). The Baseline row reports the student model with the original (un-optimized) prompt. We compare our approach with the latest optimization algorithm, GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2025). For both methods, we use Claude Sonnet 4.6 as the agent model. sections.title: 3.3 ML workflow optimization
sections.content: Settings We compare our ReASearch scaffold against Claude Code across several ML domains, including language modeling (NanoGPT), 100-class image classification (IMG100), reinforcement learning (Atari Q*bert and MuJoCo), and time series forecasting (the DRW Crypto Market Prediction Kaggle competition). We use bits per byte (BPB), accuracy, and reward as the evaluation metrics for the first four tasks, and the correlation coefficient for the crypto prediction task. For the latter, we report the score of the submitted test CSV on the private split to mirror the real Kaggle competition setting. Each experiment is run under fixed per-experiment training time budget (530 minutes depending on the task), and both ReASearch and Claude Code are given the same total wall-clock budget per task. The Claude Code baseline is the official AutoResearch setup with Claude Sonnet 4.6, used unmodified except to match our wall-clock budget; the training script, data pipeline, evaluator, hardware, and per-experiment training cap are identical on both sides. See Appendix for the matched-instruction comparison and an analysis of where the score gap comes from. We report the best result achieved under the same experiment budget in Table 6, together with the corresponding optimization curves in Figure 7. ReASearch attains stronger performance on most training tasks while using far fewer tokens. The two systems are statistically indistinguishable on NanoGPT (0.976 0.008 vs. 0.974 0.010), but ReASearch shows clear advantage on the remaining tasks. By contrast, Claude Code sometimes becomes trapped in unproductive regions of the search space and explores less efficiently. As detailed in Appendix F, which describes the matched-instruction comparison design, the gap stems from harness that re-emits the current search state (best result, recent experiments, persistent lessons, and stagnation warnings) into the prompt every turn, rather than from difference in the instructions given to the two systems. Notably, within only 15 experiments, ReASearch finds configuration that improves the submissions Kaggle leaderboard ranking from 36th to 6th (starting from baseline that already incorporates small amount of manual iteration; see Appendix H). This result highlights the practical potential of our system in realistic settings, where test labels are hidden and progress must be made under limited evaluation opportunities. Phased search with constraint-aware reasoning. Across all domains the agent consistently exhibits multi-phase optimization strategy that mirrors how human researchers approach experimental campaigns, following three-phase pattern: (i) broad architectural exploration, (ii) focused hyperparameter refinement, and (iii) diminishing-returns finetuning. In IMG-100 under 5-minute training budget, the agent first swept architectures, including WideResNet-28-10 (53.9%, too memory-heavy) and RandAugment (60.97%, too slow to converge), settling on ResNet-18 with CutMix at 65.75%. It then used python exec to 9 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 estimate wall-clock time per step (0.030.05 s), calculated that only 60100 epochs would complete in 300 seconds, and noticed the cosine learning-rate schedule was set to decay over 200 epochs, so training always stopped while the learning rate was still high. Sweeping estimated epochs confirmed the diagnosis: setting it to 100 (matching the actual epoch count) jumped accuracy from 65.75% to 79.86%, +14 percentage-point gain from single insight. Claude Code never performed this calculation and stumbled onto OneCycleLR only after dozens of wasted experiments. In Atari Q*bert, similar pattern emerged: after scaling from 8 to 16 parallel environments, the agent compared throughput (78247 steps/sec) against reward (350 both times) and concluded that learning efficiency, not data quantity was the bottleneck, leading it to deepen the FC layers (5121024512) for 5 reward jump, while Claude Code ran 90 experiments on CNN architectures without ever testing this. Diagnostic learning from failure. Rather than merely blacklisting failed configurations, the agent uses python exec to extract causal explanations that redirect subsequent search. In MuJoCo, when prioritized experience replay (PER) was proposed as standard RL improvement, the agent first benchmarked np.random.choice with priority weights against uniform np.random.randint, measured 133 slowdown, and rejected PER on computational grounds, saving an experiment that would have timed out (as Claude Code later confirmed). In IMG-100, two early EMA (exponential moving average) attempts collapsed to 1% accuracy. Rather than abandoning EMA, the agent traced the failure to batchnormalization running statistics not being propagated through naive weight averaging, then fixed it using PyTorchs AveragedModel with post-training BN recomputation, recovering +0.47% gain (83.47%83.94%). Claude Code encountered the same EMA failure and never revisited it. Discovery of co-dependent improvements. The agents most distinctive capability is detecting when parameter changes are co-dependent, i.e., improvements that only materialize when applied together, which single-parameter sweeps systematically miss. In IMG-100, AMP (mixed-precision training) appeared to be marginal speed optimization in isolation, but the agent recognized it as VRAM enabler: reducing memory from 14.3 GB to 4.1 GB made deeper architectures feasible, which in turn made CutMix augmentation beneficial (enough epochs to help rather than hurt) and EMA stable (enough capacity to regularize). This chain of co-dependent gains (82.38%84.03%) collapsed if any link was removed, as Claude Code demonstrated by never discovering AMPs enabling role, capping at 78.59%. In NanoGPT, the agent used python exec to sort all experiments by validation loss and identify near-miss improvements small enough to be independent, then combined them; critically, it discovered that reducing batch size from 218 to 217 required simultaneously retuning the learning rate (0.040.027) and warmdown schedule (0.67150.702), as applying the old hyperparameters to the new batch size would have been worse than the original configuration, trap Claude Code partially fell into by not propagating changes through dependent parameters.

sections.title: 3.4 Ablation studies
sections.content: We ablate ReASearchs core components (memory and the Python execution tool), memory design and transfer, and validation-feedback granularity. Both components matter, with memory dominating on long-trajectory prompt tasks and Python execution on ARC-AGI-2; simple what worked / what did not / what to try next schema suffices and transfers across runs; and exposing only aggregate validation metrics avoids overfitting. Full results are in Appendix C.

sections.title: 4 Conclusion
sections.content: We propose ReASearch, unified framework that turns optimization itself into reasoning problem. By replacing hand-designed search logic with agentic reasoning over tools, ReASearch enables single system to optimize prompts, programs, and ML workflows with strong empirical gains. These results suggest broader view: reasoning is not just for solving tasks, but can itself be powerful engine for open-ended search. 10 Published as conference paper at COLM

sections.title: A Related work
sections.content: LLM-based text optimization. Prior work on LLM-based text optimization typically relies on curated external heuristics to govern the overall optimization pipeline, including APE (Zhou et al., 2022), OPRO (Yang et al., 2023), ADAS (Hu et al., 2025), DGM (Zhang et al., 2025), AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025; Sharma, 2025), CodeEvolve (Assumpc ao et al., 2025), PACEvolve (Yan et al., 2026), DeltaEvolve (Jiang et al., 2026), AHE (Lin et al., 2026), and SimpleTES (Ye et al., 2026). These methods introduce range of algorithmic heuristics to guide search, such as textual-gradient-based backpropagation in DSPy, TextGrad, and AdalFlow (Khattab et al., 2023; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024; Yin & Wang, 2025); momentumbased updates (Ding et al., 2025); MCTS-based exploration in PromptAgent (Wang et al., 2023); Bayesian optimization as in MIPRO (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024; Kang & Yoganarasimhan, 2025); bandit-based allocation in ShinkaEvolve and AdaEvolve (Lange et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2026); Pareto-frontier-based selection in GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2025); and adaptive mathematical heuristics in STOP (Zelikman et al., 2023), LLaMEA (Van Stein & Back, 2024), MoH (Shi et al., 2026) and EvoX (Liu et al., 2026). Despite their algorithmic diversity, unifying limitation of these methods is their reliance on an external controller. The LLM functions merely as stateless mutation or reflection subroutine, while the actual search policy, such as budget allocation, population management, and exploration-exploitation tradeoff, is hard-coded externally. Autonomous ML Agents. More recently, autonomous agent frameworks such as AutoResearch (Karpathy, 2025; Mutable State, Inc., 2025) are closer in spirit to our approach. However, these systems primarily serve as single-domain proof-of-concepts tailored specifically for ML training pipelines, and often rely on closed-source orchestrations like Claude Code that obscure the underlying search dynamics. Crucially, they leave fundamental empirical question unanswered: to what extent can agentic reasoning serve as universal optimization policy? Our work eliminates the external controller entirely and systematically demonstrates that single, minimalist agent scaffold can internalize complex search behaviors across three fundamentally distinct optimization modalities (prompts, programs, and ML workflows). Code agents. parallel line of work equips LLMs with tools such as file editing, code execution, and terminal access for software engineering tasks, as seen in systems such as Cursor (Anysphere, Inc., 2025), Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025), OpenCode (OpenCode, 2025), and Codex (OpenAI, 2025). While these agents excel at multi-step reasoning over codebases for open-ended development, they are not inherently architected for rigid, budgetconstrained optimization loops. In our empirical evaluations, we directly benchmark ReASearch against Claude Code baseline. We demonstrate that while generalist code agents can execute experimental pipelines, they frequently struggle with constraint-aware reasoning and fall into local optima compared to reasoning-driven scaffold purpose-built for optimization. By retrofitting tool-augmented code agents into formal optimization settings, our work proves that agentic reasoning can successfully replace hand-designed mathematical meta-heuristics.

sections.title: B Extended qualitative analysis of prompt optimization
sections.content: We expand on the optimizer-like behaviors summarized in Section 3, providing concrete trajectory excerpts for each. The agent builds structured understanding of the task before optimizing. Rather than immediately generating prompt variants, the optimizer agents first invest in understanding what kinds of problems the student faces and why. On HotpotQA, the agent used python exec to parse the baseline evaluation log and categorized all 126 failures into taxonomy (categories overlap, as single failure can exhibit more than one mode): 57 verbosity cases (the student answered No, only Terence Fisher was British film director instead of simply no), 68 wrong-reasoning cases, and 8 yes/no answers polluted with explanations. This taxonomy 14 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 directly shaped the prompt: the dominant verbosity mode led to the minimum phrase framing that drove accuracy to 66.0%. Crucially, when designing subsequent candidates, the agent recalled specific previously-failing examples to verify that new fixes addressed them, e.g., checking whether ID 260 (where the student confused company with its CEO) now returned persons name after adding the rule if asked who, answer with person, not an organization. The agent verifies improvements before committing to expensive validation. Validation is the costliest operation in the budget, so the agents build confidence through cheaper channels first: inspecting student outputs on train batches, comparing error patterns across candidates, and confirming improvements happen for the right reasons. On AIME, after designing Candidate #5 with targeted math heuristics, the agent used python exec to compare all 15 remaining errors against the previous candidates 17, verifying that the antihallucination rule had eliminated known answer citations and that casework guidance reduced counting errors. Only after this content-level analysis confirmed the prompt was improving for the right reasons did the agent commit to validation. The agent autonomously navigates tree of candidates, reverting to earlier branches when path fails. Without any external controller prescribing when to backtrack, the agents maintain awareness of candidate lineage and independently decide to restart from known-good ancestor. On Terminal-Bench, after the strategy-first prompt (Candidate #3, 63.6%) was extended with three bundled refinements in Candidate #4, validation dropped by 3 points despite encouraging training scores. The agent reasoned about what specifically caused the regression (a narrower search command missed files the original had caught), reverted to Candidate #3s exact text, and added back only one sentence about heredoc formatting. This targeted addition (Candidate #5) reached 71.2%, the runs best. The revert was deliberate: the agent returned to specific node in the search tree because it understood which branch introduced the problem. The agent detects overfitting and calibrates for variance. On AIME, the agent enriched the baseline with domain-specific math heuristics and watched training accuracy climb from 60% to 66.7%, but validation returned 50.2%, below the 51.1% baseline. Rather than trying more heuristics, the agent recorded permanent lesson (domain-specific additions hurt validation generalization even when they help train) and reversed course, spending the rest of the run removing complexity. On HotpotQA, the agent re-ran the best candidates validation and obtained score 4.2 points lower, immediately recalibrating: we need consistent improvements of 35 points to be confident any change is real. The agent accumulates prompt-specific knowledge in persistent memory. In the writable lessons.md file, the agents automatically record which prompt elements help or hurt which examples, which modifications have been tried and failed, and what structural properties they have discovered about how the student model processes instructions. This accumulated knowledge directly guides later decisions: on AIME, the recorded lesson domain-specific additions hurt validation generalization even when they help train reversed the agents entire strategy from enriching prompts to simplifying them; on HotpotQA, its record of conflicting rules (use full names vs. dont repeat question nouns) prevented it from revisiting dead-end direction after context compression. The agent selects the final prompt based on the full optimization history, not just the highest score. On AIME, the agent made bolder bet: although simple baseline remained one of the best-validated prompts after 16 candidates, the agent submitted new synthesis combining the best-training candidates strengths with targeted fixes, stripped of the additions it had identified as causes of overfitting. This unvalidated prompt scored 52.0% on the 150-example test set, outperforming the best-validated prompts 49.3%, suggesting that accumulated understanding of what generalizes provided more reliable signal than validation scores alone. 15 Published as conference paper at COLM

sections.title: C Ablation studies
sections.content: Component attribution. We isolate the contribution of two core components of ReASearch by removing them while keeping all other settings unchanged: (1) the memory mechanism (lesson summaries and the search tree) and (2) the Python execution tool. Tables 7 and 8 report results on representative prompt-optimization and program-evolution tasks. Both components are important, but their relative impact varies across tasks. For prompt optimization on AIME and Terminal-Bench, the agent reads and analyzes long evaluation trajectories to identify weaknesses in the current prompt; these findings are easily lost across iterations, so memory has the larger impact. For ARC-AGI-2, where interaction rounds are shorter but pattern recognition and algorithmic discovery are central, Python execution has the larger impact, since it lets the agent reason about candidate algorithms and test them before committing. Heilbronn ablation results follow the same pattern and are reported in Appendix E. These results suggest that the components in ReASearch are not incidental tools: they support different aspects of agent-controlled search, and together let the same scaffold cover diverse optimization tasks. We study whether lessons transfer across runs by initializing new run with the lessons.md file from NanoGPT run that achieved 0.969 bpb. The new agent automatically updates the baseline and starts at 0.977, rather than the default baseline loss of about 0.998, suggesting that the memory file captures reusable optimization knowledge rather than run-specific traces. Validation feedback granularity. We ablate how much validation information is exposed during prompt optimization. Providing only the aggregate validation metric works better than exposing per-example validation trajectories, which leads to clear overfitting. On AIME, for example, performance drops from 52% to around 50% when detailed validation trajectories are revealed. Open-source backbones ReASearch is not tied to specific proprietary model: any model with sufficient longhorizon agentic ability can serve as the optimizer, and performance generally scales with the capability of the underlying model. sections.title: F Claude Code baseline details and comparison analysis
sections.content: Baseline configuration. The Claude Code baseline is the official setup in AutoResearch*. It is the standard Claude Code CLI with its full default tool surface, initialized with the upstream instruction file verbatim. That instruction file already prescribes the optimization goal, the only-edit-the-training-script rule, the per-experiment training-time budget, the keep-on-improvement / discard-on-regression loop, the simplicity criterion, and the neverstop rule. The backbone LLM is Claude Sonnet 4.6, matching ReASearch on all reported runs. The training script, data pipeline, evaluator, hardware, and per-experiment training cap are identical on both sides. Matched instructions, different harness. The instructions on the two sides say the same things. Claude Code reads Karpathys program.md (goal, only-edit-train.py rule, time budget, keep/discard loop, simplicity, NEVER-STOP, crash/VRAM guidance). ReASearchs *https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch 17 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 ML-workflow system prompt states the same goal, the same edit-train.py rule, the same time budget, the same loop (LOOP FOREVER: come up with idea edit commit run keep-or-reset), the same simplicity and NEVER-STOP rules. The phrasing differs; the content is matched. The score gap therefore does not come from ReASearch was told something Claude Code wasnt. Where the gain comes from: re-emission, not extra rules. The architectural difference is not simply that ReASearch has more instructions. The difference is where those instructions live and how often they are surfaced. Claude Code is skill-based, black-box-heavy agent system: the system prompt is fixed at conversation start, while additional information is exposed through agent-invocable surfaces such as Read/Write/Bash, MCP servers, skills, hooks, and an auto-memory file. The agent decides when to consult those surfaces; what it does not invoke, it does not see. ReASearch instead splits the same content into two layers. small static layer contains general rules and the search-loop description. The remaining state is re-emitted into the system prompt every turn: the current best result, recent experiments, persistent lessons, stagnation warnings, and structured view of the search tree. The gain comes from making search state unavoidable, rather than merely available. Concretely, five behaviors do the load-bearing work: 1. Goal and metric re-rendering. The goal, metric, and optimization direction are shown every turn, so the agent does not need to re-derive them from file. 2. Recent experiment memory. The last 20 experiments are rendered as structured table with parent, metric, memory, status, and description. This addresses longhorizon failures where agents re-try variants they had already invalidated, as in 1,800+-turn IMG-100 runs. 3. Persistent lessons. lessons.md is carried through context compaction, preserving the why of past failures, such as doubling envs didnt helpbottleneck is FC width or PER is 133 slower on this hardware. 4. Unconditional stagnation advice. After 3+ and 7+ flat evaluations, stagnation advisory is inserted directly into the prompt. This matters because an agent on plateau is unlikely to realize that it should call diagnostic tool. 5. Structured search-tree review. review search tree turns flat history into branch concentration, family distribution, and plateau signals, so the agent reads search history as structure rather than as TSV rows. This is why skills and MCP servers are not enough by themselves. They run only when the agent thinks to invoke them, which is exactly what often fails on plateaus and over long horizons. Since Claude Codes system prompt is fixed for the conversation, per-turn re-rendering is not configuration knob. Obtaining this behavior from default Claude Code setup requires rebuilding the outer loop, not merely enabling more skills. More precisely, this is not claim that Claude Codes runtime cannot host such behaviors. Its hook mechanism could, in principle, maintain stateful ledger, parse tool outputs, and re-emit structured experiment table after every turn. But realizing this through hooks layered on black-box agent is closer to engineering new framework than to configuring an existing one, and the result is the same behavior reached through heavier and less controllable route. ReASearch can be viewed as the principled form of that path: firstclass outer loop that owns prompt assembly directly, with persistent Python namespace replacing per-call shell one-shots.

sections.title: G ReASearch details
sections.content: In this section, we provide the full tool specifications exposed to the agent in our scaffold. All tasks share common set of general-purpose tools (Section G.1), and each task family adds domain-specific tools (Section G.2). 18 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 G.1 General tools The following tools are available to the agent across all task types. File I/O. The agent can read and write files within its workspace directory. read file(path): Paths are sandboxed to the workspace; directory traversal is blocked. Reading validation evaluation logs is blocked to prevent overfitting. write file(path, content): Creates parent directories as needed. list files(path): Returns file names, types, and sizes. Code execution. python exec(code): Each execution is subject to configurable timeout (default 300 s) and is logged to disk. bash(command): An extensive blocklist prevents destructive operations (e.g., rm -rf, chmod 777, pipe-to-shell patterns). Context management and memory. The agent operates under finite context window. When the conversation exceeds token threshold (default 90,000 tokens), the scaffold automatically compresses the context. The agent can also trigger this manually: compact(): The scaffold saves the full transcript to disk, calls the agent LLM to produce summary of key insights and unfinished work, then replaces the entire message history with compact 3-message sequence: an authoritative state snapshot (budget, scores, candidates), the conversation summary, and the contents of lessons.md. get status(): Each task type overrides this with domain-specific state. The agent also maintains lessons.md file in its workspace, which serves as persistent memory across context compressions. The system prompt instructs the agent to record key learnings (what worked, what didnt, what to try next) to this file, and its contents are automatically injected into the compressed context whenever compression occurs. When launching new run, lessons from previous run can be pre-loaded via --lessons flag, enabling cross-run transfer of insights. G.2 Domain-specific tools G.2.1 Prompt optimization In prompt optimization, the agent optimizes textual artifact (e.g., system prompt) for student language model. The agent is given the following tools in addition to the general tools. Each tool call consumes budget equal to the number of student-model calls it makes. get dataset info(): Get information about dataset: size, sample problem, expected answer. get next minibatch(size): Call the sampler to draw specified number of examples from the training set and return the indices. call student model batch(prompt text, sample indices): This allows the agent to test prompt drafts on customized small training subsets before committing to full validation. validate candidate(prompt text): Run evaluation on the validation set and receive only the aggregate metric, without access to the detailed trajectories. G.2.2 Program evolution In program evolution, the agent iteratively modifies Python program to optimize taskspecific score. The following domain-specific tools are provided: 19 Published as conference paper at COLM get current code(): Read the current code from solve.py. edit code(instruction): separate LLM call reads the current code and the instruction, then outputs the full modified file. This allows the agent to describe changes concisely rather than producing entire programs inline. evaluate(code text?): Evaluate the current code against the problem and get score. G.2.3 ML workflow optimization In ML workflow optimization, the agent modifies training script and runs experiments. The following domain-specific tools are provided: get current code(): Read the current code from train.py. edit train file(instruction): separate LLM call reads the current training code and the instruction, then outputs the full modified file. This allows the agent to describe changes concisely rather than producing entire programs inline. run experiment(description): Run time-bounded training job, and return the related metrics. git(command): Run git command in the task repo directory. Use for: git commit, git log, git diff, git status, git reset, git checkout. Push and remote operations are blocked.

sections.title: H Experiment settings
sections.content: H.1 Prompt optimization AIME We use 45 problems from AIME 2022, 2023, and 2024 for training and the remaining 45 for validation, repeating each validation evaluation 5 times to reduce variance. We use AIME 2025 (30 problems) as the test set and evaluate performance both before and after prompt optimization, again averaging over 5 runs. We use GPT-4.1 mini as the student model with temperature 1.0 and set the student evaluation budget to 1000. HotpotQA We use the HotpotQA dataset in the distractor setting (Yang et al., 2018), drawn from the validation split (7,405 examples). After shuffling with fixed seed, we use the first 500 examples for training, the next 500 for validation, and 1,000 for testing. Performance is measured using exact match after normalizing case, articles, and punctuation. We use GPT-4.1 mini as the student model with temperature 1.0 and set the student evaluation budget to 5000. GSM8K We use GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), taking 500 shuffled examples from the training split for optimization and another 500 for validation. The full official test split (1,319 examples) is used for testing. We use Llama 3.1 as the student model with temperature 0.7 and set the student evaluation budget to 5000. Terminal-Bench We use Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026), which comprises 89 tasks. We assign 22 tasks to training, 22 to validation, and the remaining 45 to testing, repeating both validation and test evaluations 3 times to reduce variance. Following the Terminus 2 setup, the student agent is limited to headless terminal as the single tool, and interacts with the environment exclusively through Bash commands. Tasks are evaluated via Docker-based verification with binary pass/fail outcomes. We use GPT-5 as the student model and set the student evaluation budget to 300. H.2 Program evolution Circle packing. We benchmark the max-sum variant where we place disjoint circles into unit square and maximize the sum of radii. We test from 23 to 32 (10 instances) with best known results from Friedman (2009). The agent starts from simple grid-layout baseline and evolves the packing strategy. Each evaluation runs with 600-second timeout. We report the achieved sum of radii. The maximum budget is set to 500. 20 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 Heilbronn triangle. We place points in unit square to maximize the minimum triangle area over all (n 3) triples. We test from 11 to 15 (5 instances) with the best known results from (Sudermann-Merx, 2026). The agent starts from stochastic local search baseline that perturbs points from jittered grid. Each evaluation runs with 300-second timeout. We report the achieved minimum triangle area. The maximum budget is set to 500. EPLB. We optimize the expert-parallelism load balancer for Mixture-of-Experts model, using real load trace with 288 expert replicas across 32 GPUs and 4 nodes. The agent starts from the published DeepSeek EPLB algorithm (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) and evolves the rebalancing strategy. Each evaluation simulates inference across sliding windows and runs with 360-second timeout. We report composite score: (bexpert + sspeed)/2, where bexpert measures load balancedness and sspeed = 0.002/tinference. The maximum budget is set to 500. Transaction scheduling. We schedule 3 workloads of 100 database transactions each to minimize the total makespan, subject to read/write conflict dependencies. The agent starts from greedy cost-sampled scheduler baseline and evolves the scheduling strategy. Each evaluation runs with 600-second timeout. We report the total makespan across all three workloads. The maximum budget is set to 500. ARC-AGI-2. We use 120 puzzles from the ARC-AGI-2 evaluation set (Chollet et al., 2025). For each puzzle, the agent writes two transformation functions (transform grid attempt 1 and transform grid attempt 2) that map input grids to output grids based on few training examples. The agent starts from dummy placeholder baseline (rotation + color increment) that must be completely rewritten. Each evaluation runs both attempts with 60-second timeout. We report accuracy (pass@2): puzzle is solved if either attempt exactly matches the expected output. The maximum budget is set to 500. H.3 ML workflow optimization NanoGPT. The agent improves GPT language model in the NanoGPT setting (Karpathy, 2022), minimizing validation bits per byte (val bpb). The time budget is 5 minutes with 10-minute experiment timeout. IMG-100. The agent improves image classification on IMG-100, maximizing accuracy on the validation set. The baseline is ResNet-18. The time budget is 5 minutes with 10-minute experiment timeout. Atari. The agent improves deep RL policies for the Q*bert environment, maximizing evaluation reward averaged over 10 episodes. The baseline is PPO with 30-minute time budget and 40-minute experiment timeout. MuJoCo. The agent improves continuous control policies on HalfCheetah, maximizing evaluation reward averaged over 10 episodes. All environments use SAC as the baseline algorithm. The time budget is 10 minutes with 15-minute experiment timeout. DRW - Crypto Market Prediction The agent optimizes models for an anonymized crypto trading dataset with 785 features and approximately 525K training examples, using validation Pearson correlation (val corr) as the optimization objective. We begin from 6fold cross-validation baseline that ensembles linear model and an MLP, whose submission ranks 36th on the Kaggle leaderboard. We then perform small amount of manual iteration and leaderboard submission, distill the resulting lessons into the agent instructions, and allow the agent to continue optimizing from there. This setup is intended to mimic realistic Kaggle competition workflow. https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/drw-crypto-market-prediction 21 Published as conference paper at COLM

sections.title: I Optimization artifacts and agent lessons
sections.content: We present the full prompts (before and after optimization) for each prompt optimization task for both ReASearch and GEPA, and the summarized agents self-written lessons.md files across all task categories. These lessons are maintained by the agent throughout each run and survive context compression; they serve as the agents persistent memory of what worked, what didnt, and what to try next. I.1 Prompt optimization I.1.1 AIME Baseline prompt. Solve the problem and provide the answer in the correct format. Reasoning: Let's think step by step in order to solve this problem. After your reasoning, output your final answer as ### where is an integer (0-999). ReASearch optimized prompt. You are solving an AIME-style math problem. Compute single integer with 0 <= <= 999, then output exactly one final line: ### Method (concise and exact): - Clarify the target: Restate exactly what is asked, for example reduced m/n then m+n; least nonnegative residue; total number of labeled configurations; length or area leading to m*sqrt(n) then m+n. Re-read the last sentence before finalizing. - Exact math only: use integers, fractions, and radicals with square-free parts; rationalize when needed. No decimal approximations unless rounding is requested. Do not cite "known answers" or use code. - Track constraints: ordered vs unordered; labeled vs unlabeled, and count all labeled configurations unless symmetry reduction is explicitly required; distinctness; parity; digit/base bounds; coprimality; domains. - AIME toolkit: algebra/factorization; Vieta/discriminants; modular arithmetic; complementary counting/inclusion-exclusion; invariants/symmetry; exact geometry including similarity, Power of Point, Ptolemy, mass points, and clean coordinates. - Patterns: If p(m)=p(k), write p(x)-p(k)=(x-k)r(x); analyze with Vieta/discriminant and enforce integer/uniqueness by bounded casework. - Prefer finite casework when ranges are small, such as digits or small divisors; set up explicit constraints rather than guessing. - Validate any derived formula on at least two simple cases, including edge or given examples; if test fails, fix the derivation. Final checklist: 1) Target match: reduced m/n before m+n; least nonnegative residue; square-free radicals before m+n; count labeled objects unless told otherwise; correct object and complete case coverage. 2) is single integer in [0,999]. 3) Sanity checks: parity/mod and magnitude bounds; quick plug-back when feasible. 4) Output exactly one line: ### with no extra text after. GEPA optimized prompt. 22 Published as conference paper at COLM Task: You will be given single contest-style math problem. Solve it exactly and output ONLY the final numeric answer as bare integer with no extra text, symbols , or formatting. Output format (strict): - Output only the final integer. - No words, labels, LaTeX, boxes, units, punctuation, or trailing/leading zeros. - Examples of valid outputs: 756, 751, 73. - Examples of invalid outputs: boxed{756}, 073, 756., Answer: 756. Core directives: - Read the prompt carefully to identify exactly what quantity is requested (e.g., ACˆ2 instead of AC; or m+n for fraction m/n in lowest terms). - Keep all computations exact (no decimal rounding). Use radicals, fractions, and exact integers as needed until the final step. - If the problem defines fraction m/n with and relatively prime, fully reduce the fraction before computing m+n. - If squared length is requested, compute it directly (avoid unnecessary square roots). - Perform quick consistency checks for reasonableness before finalizing. - Use bounding/degree checks to prune impossible contributions in sums/series/ polynomials. - If the problem asks for sum of squares or similar aggregate, compute exactly and only at the end. - If multiple cases are possible, ensure the answer satisfies all given conditions; eliminate extraneous solutions. General problem-solving guidance: - Introduce substitution to simplify structure (e.g., set = log_b n, or parameterize = eˆ{itheta}). - Use symmetry, parity, and monotonicity to reduce cases. - For constrained optimization on circles/spheres, convert to linear forms and use Cauchy--Schwarz or distance-to-line interpretation. - For medians and modes in integer lists, relate list length parity to median definition; enforce uniqueness conditions on frequencies. Domain-specific strategies and facts: 1) Geometry with spheres and cutting plane: - For spheres of radii r_i with centers O_i, intersected by plane in congruent circles of radius with all centers on the same side of the plane: xˆ2 = r_iˆ2 - h_iˆ2 with h_i > 0 where h_i is the perpendicular distance from O_i to the plane. - If A, are the projections of O_i, O_j onto the plane (centers of the intersection circles), then: ABˆ2 = O_iO_jˆ2 - (h_i - h_j)ˆ2. - If spheres are mutually externally tangent, then O_iO_j = r_i + r_j. - Use given planar distances (e.g., ABˆ2) to solve for xˆ2 and h_i; then compute any requested planar distances via the same ABˆ2 relation. 2) Cube geometry with tilted orientation and horizontal water surface: - vertical face can be used to model linear variation of vertex heights above the horizontal plane; heights vary linearly along edges. - Determine the cube side length from given vertex heights using orthogonality or similar triangles; in known analogous setup, = 6. - Volume with horizontal plane at height h: the empty region above the water may be frustum between two parallel planar sections. Use: V_frustum = (H/3) * (A1 + sqrt(A1*A2) + A2), where is the separation along the normal inside the solid, and A1, A2 are the cross-sectional areas at the two levels. - Practical approach: compute the full cube volume sˆ3; compute the empty frustum volume by identifying cross-sectional squares that scale linearly; subtract from ˆ3. 3) Set counting with "everyone owns" one item and exact-count constraints: 23 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 - If all people own universal item H, and other items A, B, have totals A, B, C; let w, x, y, be the counts owning exactly 1, 2, 3, 4 items (including H). - Then: + + + = N, + 2x + 3y + 4z = where = + + + and = N. - If some of w, x, y, are given, solve the linear system to find the desired count ( e.g., z). 4) Rectangles in regular 2n-gon (e.g., dodecagon): - Rectangles correspond to choosing two distinct pairs of opposite vertices. In regular dodecagon, there are 6 opposite pairs; each rectangle is determined by two of these pairs. - Model as 2x6 grid by pairing opposite vertices as columns; rectangles correspond to 2x2 submatrices formed by two columns. - For 2-colorings avoiding monochromatic rectangle: - Column types are (top,bottom) in {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)}. - Types (0,0) and (1,1) may appear at most once each; (0,1) and (1,0) may repeat freely. - Casework for dodecagon yields total of 928 valid colorings. 5) Coefficients in generating functions of the form P(x) = (xˆN - 1)ˆk / prod(xˆ{m_i} - 1) for 0 < < 1: - Use 1/(xˆm - 1) = -1/(1 - xˆm) = -sum_{t>=0} xˆ{mt} and expand (xˆN - 1)ˆk = sum_{ j=0}ˆk (-1)ˆ{k-j} C(k, j) xˆ{Nj}. - If the target exponent satisfies < N, then only = 0 contributes. - Reduce to counting nonnegative integer solutions of sum m_i t_i = via modular reductions and = lcm(m_i); often becomes stars-and-bars count for the multiple -of-L part after fixing residues. - Example: With m_i in {105,70,42,30} and = 2022 (< 2310), count solutions to 105b + 70c + 42d + 30e = 2022; successive modular reductions lead to b' + c' + d' + e' = 9, giving C(12,3) = 220. 6) River-crossing with current and equidistant target on opposite bank: - Let be downstream and across the river; current adds (v_c, 0) to each swimmer's water-relative velocity. - If swimmers start at (0,0) and (D,0) and meet simultaneously at (D/2, W) in time T: - Vertical components satisfy v_y = W/T. - Ground-velocity x-components include current; magnitude constraints yield two equations in unknowns. - Subtract to eliminate squares, giving linear relation = for constant c; then use = v_y to solve for and compute D. 7) Complex numbers: maximizing the real part with fixed: - For expressions of the form Re(A + B/z) with = r: - Use 1/z = conjugate(z)/zˆ2 = (1/r) eˆ{-itheta} if = eˆ{itheta}. - Then Re(A eˆ{itheta} + (B/r) eˆ{-itheta}) becomes linear combination cos theta + sin theta; the maximum is sqrt(pˆ2 + qˆ2). - Equivalent approach: set = + bi with aˆ2 + bˆ2 = rˆ2; express the real part as + and maximize via Cauchy--Schwarz: max = sqrt(Pˆ2 + Qˆ2). - Tangent-to-circle distance method gives the same maximum. 8) Integer lists with sum, unique mode, and "median is an integer not in the list": - If the median is an integer but not in the list, the list length must be even. The median equals (a_m + a_{m+1})/2, an integer that must not appear as any element. - The two middle elements must have the same parity (their average is an integer). common minimal pattern is they differ by 2 so the average is the in-between integer not present. - Unique mode "9" means the count of 9's is strictly greater than the count of any other value; avoid ties (e.g., do not allow another value to occur as often as 9). - For small total sum constraints, start with the smallest even length that can realize the requirements (often n=4). With sum 30 and unique mode 9: - Two 9's force the remaining two numbers to sum to 12 and be less than 9 to prevent median 9. - To make the median an integer not in the list, choose the two to be (5,7) (not (6,6), which breaks uniqueness of the mode). 24 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 - Then compute the requested aggregate (e.g., sum of squares 5ˆ2 + 7ˆ2 + 9ˆ2 + 9ˆ2 = 236). 9) Logarithmic equations with base != 1: - Let = log_b to linearize expressions. Use log_b(nˆk) = log_b and log_b(bn) = 1 + log_b n. - Respect domains: sqrt(log_b n) requires log_b >= 0. - Example: sqrt(x) = x/2 and = 1 + => in {0,4}, discard x=0 if it breaks the second equation; with x=4 obtain = (1+x)/x = 5/4 and = bˆx = (5/4)ˆ4 = 625/256; reduce before computing j+k. Process checks: - Confirm all constraints (parity, domain, uniqueness, ranges) are satisfied by the final candidate. - Discard extraneous roots introduced by squaring or by implicit domain violations. - For expressions requiring maximum/minimum, justify that the found value is achievable. Final step: - After verifying correctness, output only the final integer as specified above. Agent lessons. ## What Worked - Baseline system prompt (#1) achieved 51.1% on val (mean over 5 runs). On train, it scored 27/45 = 60%. Formatting was generally correct. - Cand5_prompt (Candidate #3) performed best on train: 66.7%. Key elements: - exact arithmetic (no decimals), - target clarity and strict final checklist, - pattern guidance for p(m)=p(k) via factoring and Vieta/discriminant, - finite casework for small ranges. ## What Didn't Work - Cand7_prompt added early parity/mod checks and Euler/arrangement guidance, but validation dropped to 45.8% -- overloading/overfitting hurt generalization. - Cand2_prompt regressed to 48.9%, with hallucinated "known answers," decimal approximations, and out-of-range outputs. - Cand8_prompt tried to hard-code cubic uniqueness, but train slipped to 53.3%. Strong assertions may be wrong in some cases or too prescriptive. ## Key Lessons - The baseline is already near-optimal for AIME with this student model. - Domain-specific add-ons consistently degraded val performance. - Adding rules that help specific train problems tends to hurt generalization. I.1.2 HotpotQA Baseline prompt. You are question answering assistant. You will be given context documents and question. Read the documents carefully and answer the question. Output your final answer as ### <answer> on its own line. ReASearch optimized prompt. Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 You are an expert question answering assistant for multi-hop reasoning tasks. You will be given several context documents and question that requires reasoning across multiple documents. ## Your Task Read all documents carefully, then answer the question by following the chain of reasoning across documents. ## Reasoning Process **Step 1 -- Build the reasoning chain**: Multi-hop questions require connecting facts across multiple documents. Trace each step: what does document tell you? How does that connect to document B? Follow the chain to the FINAL answer. **Step 2 -- Determine the answer type from the question**: - "Who..." -> person's name (use the full name as it appears in the document, including middle names) - "Which [entity]..." -> the name of that specific entity - "How many..." -> the number or quantity - "What [year/date]..." -> the year or date - "What [title/name/role/type/kind]..." -> the exact title, name, role, or type - "Is/Are/Was/Were/Did/Does/Can..." -> "yes" or "no" only **Step 3 -- Extract the answer span**: Find the exact phrase in the documents that answers the question. The answer should be: - direct quote from the document (verbatim) - The MINIMUM phrase that fully answers the question - Not full sentence -- just the answer itself - Not surrounded by extra context words **Step 4 -- Verify your answer**: - Does it directly answer what the question asks? - Is it the right type? Check carefully: - If asked "who" -> must be person's name, not an organization or place - If asked "what kind/type/genre" -> must be category, not specific instance - If asked "which [film/book/team]" -> must be the name of that thing - If asked "what year" -> must be year (or date) - Have you stopped at the right point -- not too much, not too little? ## Key Rules - **Yes/No questions**: Answer ONLY "yes" or "no" -- nothing else. - **Comparison questions** (who is older/bigger/has more X): give the NAME of the winning entity, not the value. - **Full names**: Use the complete name as it appears in the document, including middle names. - **No extra context**: Do not add "by [author]", "in [place]", or other surrounding words. - **No paraphrase**: Copy the exact wording from the document. - **Don't drop words**: Keep all words that are part of the answer. ## Format Think through the reasoning step by step, then output your final answer on its own line as: ### <answer> The answer after ### should contain ONLY the answer itself. GEPA optimized prompt. You are question answering assistant. You will be given context documents and question. Read the documents carefully and answer the question. Give short, concise answer (typically 1-3 words). 26 Published as conference paper at COLM Important guidelines: 1. Base your answer strictly on the information provided in the documents. 2. When the question asks about specific detail, find the exact phrasing used in the relevant document and use that as your answer. 3. Pay close attention to the exact wording in the documents. Use the most specific or complete form of the answer as it appears in the text (e.g., full names, exact titles, precise terms). 4. If person's full name is given in the document (e.g., "Masayoshi 'Masa' Takayama" ), use the complete name as written, not shortened version. 5. If disease or term has multiple names in the document (e.g., "amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), commonly known as 'Lou Gehrig's Disease'"), use the name that best matches the phrasing of the question or the most commonly referenced form in the document. 6. Do not paraphrase, summarize, or infer beyond what is explicitly stated in the documents. 7. If the question references nickname or alternate name, map it to the full name as given in the document. Agent lessons. ## Improvement Chain - Baseline (#1): 8.8% - V2 (#2): 21.2% -- structured approach + yes/no instruction - V4 (#4): 60.0% -- question-type awareness, verbatim extraction, full names - V5 (#5): 65.0% -- question-type guidance (who->person, which->entity) - V10 (#10): 66.0% -- "MINIMUM phrase" framing, verify step - V14 (#14): 68.0% -- explicit type-mismatch checks in verify step ## What Made #14 the Best Compared to #10 (66%), #14 added to the verify step: - "If asked 'who' -> must be person's name, not an organization or place" - "If asked 'what kind/type/genre' -> must be category, not specific instance" These explicit type-mismatch checks pushed from 66% to 68%. ## What Hurt (every modification to #14 degraded val) - Removing "use full names" rule: 65% -> 62.8% - Adding stronger anti-verbosity rules: 65% -> 61.2% - Adding worked examples: 65% -> 62.2% - Shorter/simpler prompt: 66% -> 57% (MAJOR REGRESSION) - Adding "how many -> number only without units": 68% -> 66.8% - Adding "don't repeat question nouns": 68% -> 65.6% - Adding "Re-read question": 68% -> 66.0% ## Key Insights - The detailed 4-step structure is CRITICAL -- shorter prompts hurt significantly. - Train batch scores are VERY NOISY -- #17 showed 70% vs 65% on train but 66% vs 68% on val. - Adding rules tends to hurt: every time we add specific rules, they help some cases but hurt others. - Dataset is inconsistent: sometimes needs full name, sometimes common name. - We are at local optimum with #14: every modification tried has hurt on val. I.1.3 GSM8K Baseline prompt. Solve the math problem step by step. Show your work clearly. After your reasoning, output your final numerical answer as ### where is the number (e.g., ### 42). 27 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 ReASearch optimized prompt. You are an expert math tutor solving grade-school math word problems. Solve each problem carefully and accurately. ## Your Approach: 1. **Read carefully**: Identify all given quantities and what the question is asking for. 2. **Plan**: Break the problem into clear steps. 3. **Solve**: Work through each step, showing calculations. 4. **Verify**: Check that your answer makes sense. Ask: Is the answer positive when it should be? Is it in the right direction (e.g., "lost by N" means subtract, not add)? If you get different result when re-checking, carefully identify the specific error before changing your answer. ## Common Pitfalls to Avoid: - "X times more than Y" means X*Y more, so the total is + X*Y = (X+1)*Y - "X times fewer/less" means divide by (e.g., "3 times fewer" = 1/3 of the amount) - "cuts X% off" means the remainder is (100-X)% of the original - "90% less" means 10% of the original remains - Rate problems: if workers take time, then 2N workers take T/2 time (inverse relationship) - Percentages applied sequentially: apply each to the running total, not the original - Re-read the question: make sure you're answering what was actually asked ## Output Format: After your solution, you MUST end your response with your final numerical answer on its own line in this exact format: ### where is the number (e.g., ### 42 or ### 3.5) Do not skip this final line. Always end with ### N. GEPA optimized prompt. Solve the math word problem step by step. Show your work clearly at each step. Follow these guidelines: 1. Read the problem carefully and identify all the quantities, relationships, and operations needed. 2. Break the problem into sequential steps, performing one operation at time. 3. At each step, clearly state what you are calculating and why. 4. Be careful to track which quantities apply to which groups (e.g., if population grows, the new total becomes the base for the next calculation). 5. Watch for multi-stage problems where results from one stage feed into the next stage - make sure to use the updated totals, not the original starting values. 6. Pay close attention to language like "each" - when it says each member of group does something, multiply by the CURRENT total count of that group, not just the original count. 7. For problems involving sequences or arithmetic progressions, set up an algebraic equation and solve systematically. 8. For age problems: carefully identify the time reference (e.g., "two years ago", "in five years"). Work out each person's age at the specified point in time, apply any given relationships (e.g., "twice as old") at THAT point in time, and then adjust forward or backward to find the present-day age. Do NOT mix up ages from different points in time. 9. For percentage problems: calculate the percentage of the given base value, then apply the result (add or subtract) as directed. 10. Double-check your arithmetic at each step before moving on. 28 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 11. After completing all steps, state your final answer clearly. After your reasoning, output your final numerical answer as ### where is the number (e.g., ### 42). Agent lessons. ## Improvement Chain - Baseline (#1): 88.4% - V2 (#2): 90.2% (+1.8%) -- structured 4-step + pitfalls + ## headers - V2-sanity (#9): 90.4% (+0.2%) -- Verify step direction check - V9-language (#10): 90.6% (+0.2%) -- "X times fewer/less = divide by X" pitfall - V10-verify-trust (#21): 90.8% (+0.2%) -- "if re-check gives different result, identify specific error before changing answer" ## Verify Step Wording Matters Critically - #21: "If you get different result when re-checking, carefully identify the specific error before changing your answer" -> 90.8% - #22: "Trust your step-by-step work -- only change your answer if you can point to specific error" -> 88.0% - The difference: #21 says "identify the error" (implies look for it), #22 says "trust your work" (implies don't change). "Trust your work" is too strong -- prevents legitimate corrections. ## "Pitfall Saturation" Effect -- CONFIRMED After 7 pitfall bullets, adding ANY more consistently hurts (13+ attempts, all worse). The model has limited attention for instructions; more pitfalls cause confusion. The sweet spot is exactly the 7 pitfalls in #21. ## Key Failure Mode Discovered - Model correctly computed 40 (Alia markers problem) - Verify step caused model to re-compute with different logic -> got 80 (WRONG) - Fix: Added warning to identify specific error before changing answer - This fix improved val from 90.6% -> 90.8% ## ALL 13 modifications to #21 HURT (range: -1.0% to -2.8%) - NEVER conclude prompt is better based on single train batch. - Strong evidence of global optimum at #21 for this prompt structure. I.1.4 Terminal-Bench Baseline prompt. You are an expert software engineer and Linux terminal user. You are working inside Docker container to solve tasks. For each task, you will receive instructions and can execute bash commands. Output each command in ```bash code block. You will see the stdout/stderr output after each command. Work step by step: 1. Read the task carefully 2. Explore the environment (ls, cat, etc.) 3. Implement the solution 4. Verify your work 5. When done, respond with: DONE ReASearch optimized prompt. Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 You are an expert software engineer and Linux terminal user. You are working inside Docker container to solve tasks. For each task, you will receive instructions and can execute bash commands. Output each command in ```bash code block. You will see the stdout/stderr output after each command. ## Strategy **Before implementing anything:** 1. Explore the environment: `ls -la /app` and read all relevant files 2. Find test/check scripts: `find / -maxdepth 4 -name "test*" -o -name "check*" -o - name "verify*" 2>/dev/null grep -v proc` 3. Read the test scripts to understand EXACTLY what is being checked **Implementation:** 4. Implement the solution based on what the tests require 5. Run the tests -- if they fail, read the error and fix the root cause 6. Repeat until tests pass **Before DONE:** - Confirm your solution actually works (run tests, check output files exist, verify services are running) - Only say DONE when you are confident the solution is correct ## Important Rules - **Install missing tools**: `apt-get install -y <package>` or `pip install <package>` - **Heredoc safety**: The closing delimiter (EOF, PY, etc.) must be on its OWN line with NOTHING after it - **Background services**: After starting, verify with `curl http://localhost:PORT` or `ps aux grep <name>` - **Long tasks**: If command might timeout, run it with `timeout 300 <command>` and check exit code When done, respond with: DONE GEPA optimized prompt. You are an expert software engineer and Linux terminal user working inside Docker container. You will receive short task name (e.g., train-fasttext, mcmc-sampling -stan, compile-compcert, crack-7z-hash, build-cython-ext, bn-fit-modify, chessbest-move, git-multibranch). Execute bash commands step by step and print each command in single ```bash code block; you will see stdout/stderr after each command. When you need to create multi-line files or run inline Python/R code, use proper here-docs with the closing token on its own line and no extra spaces. Do not include stray backticks inside command blocks. Avoid chaining too many operations in one long command to prevent here-doc parsing errors; split into multiple commands. Always verify results and end with DONE.
